# Object-Oriented Testbench Design {#sec-ch06}

*A base class fixes an algorithm and leaves named holes; a test fills one.*

::: {.callout-note title="Learning objectives"}
After this chapter you can derive a class from another and say what `super.new` must do and when; predict which method body a call runs, through which handle, and say why `virtual` changes the answer; declare an abstract class and an interface class and choose between them; cast down a hierarchy safely and copy an object without losing its type; read a parameterized class as a family of distinct types and name the consequences that has in a testbench; recognize the one idea under the factory, strategy, template-method, singleton and callback patterns and find each in a testbench that exists; state the substitution property that decides whether a subclass is a subtype; and say, for every construct here, which of the book's two simulators runs it and which runs it and prints the wrong answer.
:::

## One object, three answers

One leaf object. Three handles naming it, declared as the leaf's class, its parent and its grandparent. One virtual method, asked the same question through each. The language's answer is one number three times, because a virtual call is dispatched on the object, not on the declaration of the handle it came through. Here is what the book's two simulators say:

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch06-oop-testbench-design/three-handles/tb_three_handles.sv"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch06-oop-testbench-design/three-handles/run.out"}
```

The event-driven simulator gave three different answers and compiled the file without a warning. Its tracker records why, in a maintainer's words: "The virtual keyword is accepted by the parser, but otherwise ignored. This is also true for virtual methods." [@icarus-issue-421] A testbench built on virtual methods and run there does not fail; it runs an ancestor's code wherever a base handle appears and reports that everything passed. @sec-ch05-tools measured that cell once; this chapter is where it matters, because every construct from here to the end of Part III depends on `virtual` doing what the standard says.

So this chapter's examples run on Verilator, and where a listing runs on both tools it is to print the silent answer beside the right one. The rest of the chapter is what `virtual` is *for*.

## Extending a class {#sec-ch06-extends}

A class extends another with `extends`, and the derived class is the base plus what it adds. Its constructor must reach the base's constructor first. The rules are three. Both of this book's compilers state two of them in their diagnostics: a `super.new` call must be the first statement of the derived constructor, and when the derived constructor says nothing an implicit `super.new()` with no arguments is called, which is itself an error if the base constructor needs one. The third is the standard's alone here: the `extends` clause may carry the constructor arguments instead, and then an explicit `super.new` is an error [@ieee1800-2023] — a form the Verilator this book runs does not yet parse, so the listings use `super.new`.

The other thing a derived class does is redeclare a method the base already has, and the word `virtual` on the base's declaration decides what that means. Without it, the derived method *hides* the base's: a call through a base handle still runs the base body. With it, the derived method *overrides*: the call runs the derived body whatever the handle's declared type.

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch06-oop-testbench-design/extends-chain/tb_extends.sv"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch06-oop-testbench-design/extends-chain/run.out"}
```

Through `p`, the base handle, `describe` runs the base body and prints no code, while `tag` runs the derived body: the first was hidden and the second overridden, and the only difference between them in the source is one word.

## What `virtual` changes {#sec-ch06-virtual}

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
A **virtual method** is dispatched on the run-time class of the object, not on the declared class of the handle. A call through a base handle to a virtual method runs the most-derived override the object has. A call to a non-virtual method runs the body the handle's declared class sees [@ieee1800-2023].
:::

That one rule is what lets a testbench be written *once*. A driver's loop — reset, get a transaction, drive it, repeat — is the same for every protocol; what one transaction looks like on the wires is not. Put the loop in a base class as an ordinary method, put the per-transaction step in the same class as a virtual method with a default body, and a derived driver changes the step without touching the loop. Gamma and colleagues call this shape the template method [@gamma1994patterns]; a verification engineer meets it before knowing its name, because it is how a UVM component's phases work — `run_phase` and its siblings are virtual methods the library calls and the user overrides [@uvm-core-component] — and it is the shape of OpenTitan's base driver, whose `run_phase` forks a reset handler and a get-and-drive loop that its derived drivers fill in [@opentitan-dv-lib].

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch06-oop-testbench-design/template-method/tb_template.sv"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch06-oop-testbench-design/template-method/run.out"}
```

The derived handle is the only handle in that file, and the event-driven simulator still ran the base's step, because the call to `step` is made from base-class code and that tool binds every call to the class whose code makes it. The template method is the shape that tool gets wrong even when no base handle appears anywhere.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall"}
One more shape, which both of this book's tools handle the same way and which is worth avoiding on any: a virtual method called from the *base* class's constructor. The derived part of the object has not been constructed when the base constructor runs, so whatever an override reads there is not yet set. Both of this book's simulators run the base body in that case; the standard's text on the point was not consulted for this book, and the guidance does not need it: do not call a virtual method from a constructor.
:::

## Abstract classes and interface classes {#sec-ch06-abstract}

Sometimes the base class has no sensible default for a step — a shape has no area until it is a particular shape — and the honest declaration is a `pure virtual` method: a promise every concrete subclass must keep, in a class that cannot itself be constructed, which is what `virtual class` declares. An `interface class` is the same promise with nothing else: no data, no bodies, only method signatures, and a class `implements` as many of them as it likes while it `extends` at most one base [@ieee1800-2023].

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch06-oop-testbench-design/abstract-interface/tb_abstract.sv"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch06-oop-testbench-design/abstract-interface/run.out"}
```

The choice between them is that one difference. Extend a base for shared state and shared code; implement an interface class for a shared contract that unrelated classes can each keep. A scoreboard that can compare anything printable does not care what else the thing is.

::: {.callout-tip title="In Practice"}
UVM's base object declares `create` and `get_type_name` as promises in its documentation and gives them default bodies in its source: the contract is a convention the registration macros satisfy, not a `pure virtual` the compiler enforces [@uvm-core-object]. That is the pattern to expect in a library that predates interface classes, and the reason a class that forgets its registration macro compiles and then fails at run time.
:::

## Casting down, copying across {#sec-ch06-cast-copy}

Assigning a derived handle to a base handle needs no cast, because the object is a base object and more. Going the other way asks a question the compiler cannot answer — is the object behind this base handle really one of those? — so `$cast` asks it at run time, and answers no by returning zero and leaving the target handle untouched [@ieee1800-2023].

Copying is where the type is lost. `new src` copies the object *the handle's declared type says is there*; on the Verilator this book measures, a base handle holding a derived object yields a base object, and a virtual call on the copy runs the base body [@verilator-issue-7105]. The fix landed in Verilator's 5.046 release, sixteen months after the 5.030 this book runs [@verilator-changes]. A copy that keeps its type is a virtual method that constructs its own class — every override of `clone` calls its own `new` — which is what UVM's `clone` does, calling `create` to construct the right class and then `copy` to fill it, with a virtual `do_copy` hook whose overrides must call `super.do_copy` so each level copies its own fields [@uvm-core-object].

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch06-oop-testbench-design/cast-clone/tb_cast_clone.sv"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch06-oop-testbench-design/cast-clone/run.out"}
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall"}
`new base` printed `packet` for an object that is an `error_packet`. Nothing warned. The other tool cannot run that line at all — its runtime aborts on a shallow copy through a base handle, which the table below records as *no run* — and gets the next one wrong: its `clone`, being virtual, binds to the handle's declared type and returns a base object too. A scoreboard that stores copies made that way compares base fields only and never sees the error code; a test that passes on this tool and fails on a newer one has found the difference between a copy and a clone.
:::

## Parameterized classes as a design tool {#sec-ch06-param}

A parameterized class is a family. `box #(int)` and `box #(string)` are not two views of one class but two classes, each its own type, each with its own static members and its own place in the hierarchy [@ieee1800-2023].

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch06-oop-testbench-design/param-classes/tb_param.sv"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch06-oop-testbench-design/param-classes/run.out"}
```

Two specializations, two counters. That rule is what makes typed composition possible — a driver parameterized by its transaction type holds a `T` and not a base handle, and the compiler checks every use — and it has three consequences a UVM testbench meets. A configuration database parameterized by type keeps one pool per specialization in its source, which is why a value set through `uvm_config_db #(int)` is not found by a read through `uvm_config_db #(bit [31:0])` [@uvm-core]; lowRISC's guide, for the related reason that basic types collide in a shared namespace, allows only configuration objects through it [@lowrisc-dv-style]. A factory that creates by type hands back a base-class handle, so the caller must `$cast` the result to the specialization it declared — unconditionally, as OpenTitan's base test does for its configuration type [@opentitan-dv-base-test]. And the registration macro for a parameterized class registers no type *name*, so the operations that find a class by its name string — a test selected on the command line, an override by name — cannot see it [@accellera2015uvmref].

::: {.callout-tip title="In Practice"}
OpenTitan's base driver is parameterized by its transaction and configuration types, and its own source says it would make more sense as an abstract class with a pure virtual get-and-drive, and cannot be one because the agent that holds it constructs the default driver type unless a test overrides the parameter [@opentitan-dv-lib]. That is the cost of the family in one sentence: a default type is a type something will build.
:::

## One idea, five patterns {#sec-ch06-patterns}

The patterns a testbench is built from have names, four of them from Gamma and colleagues' catalog — factory, strategy, template method, singleton [@gamma1994patterns] — and the fifth, the callback, is the same idea with the hook made an object. One idea is under all of them. A base class fixes an algorithm and leaves named holes, and a test fills a hole without editing the algorithm. What differs is which hole:

- **Which class** to construct: the *factory*. The environment asks for an object by a base type and gets whatever the test substituted. UVM's factory does this by type and by instance, with overrides that a test installs before the environment builds [@accellera2015uvmug]; its class reference adds the by-name forms [@accellera2015uvmref].
- **What a step does**: the *template method* above, and its cousin the *strategy*, where the step is a separate object handed in rather than a method overridden. UVM's comparison, printing and packing policies are strategies passed as arguments [@accellera2015uvmref], and the 1800.2 library added a copier alongside them [@uvm-core-object].
- **Knob values**: a *configuration object* the environment reads and the test writes.
- **Behavior in a component the test does not own**: a *callback*, a hook object the component calls at a named point, so a test adds a check to a driver it cannot subclass because someone else's test already did.
- **One of something**: the *singleton* — a root, a resource database — reached through a static `get()`.

Every one of those is visible in code the reader can open: the driver's `run_phase` in OpenTitan's DV library is the template method, five lines long, with its mandatory and optional hooks described in its comments [@opentitan-dv-lib]; UVM's core-service object is the singleton, with a setter that is the seam a test uses to substitute one [@uvm-core]. The worked example below builds three of them on one FIFO: the factory, the template method and the callback.

### The singleton, and what it costs

A testbench has one root and one configuration database because a component asks for them without being told where they are. The price is the one everything global costs: a test that wants two environments with two databases has to unpick a decision the library made once. UVM's core service has a setter through which a test substitutes one without editing the library [@uvm-core]; a testbench that reaches the database directly has given the option away.

## When a subclass is not a subtype {#sec-ch06-lsp}

Inheritance lets a derived object stand in for a base one wherever the base is expected. Whether it *should* is a different question, and Liskov's formulation is the one to carry: an object of the derived type must be usable wherever an object of the base type is, without the program that uses it being able to tell the difference [@liskov1987hierarchy]. In verification terms, a derived transaction must still be a legal transaction. Adding a constraint keeps that — every randomized instance the derived class produces is one the base class could have produced. Loosening a constraint breaks it, and so does an override of a comparison that forgets to call `super`, because the base's fields are no longer compared. The factory will substitute either kind without complaint: UVM's requirement is that the override be polymorphically compatible with the original, which is a statement about types, not about contracts [@accellera2015uvmug]; lowRISC's rule that a sequence item must result in a legal transaction when randomized is that contract stated for one class of object, and it binds a derived item as much as its base [@lowrisc-dv-style].

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall"}
Deep hierarchies fail this test by accumulation: each level's override of `do_compare` or `do_copy` that forgets `super` drops one level's fields, and nothing reports it. The advice against inheriting for code reuse rather than for substitution is not specific to this language — a widely used style guide says to prefer composition and to keep inheritance for the case where the derived object *is* one of the base [@google-cpp-style] — and a transaction class is the place a testbench most often ignores it.
:::

## What runs where {#sec-ch06-tools}

The table below is @sec-ch05-tools's table for this chapter's constructs: one probe per row, run under Verilator with the flags the book's build uses and under Icarus with `-g2012`, a row saying *runs* only if the probe printed the values it expected. It is regenerated on every build by the same runner @sec-ch05-tools ships, with this chapter's probes.

{{< include /examples/ch06-oop-testbench-design/support-matrix/matrix.md >}}

Two columns of it are the chapter's argument. Every virtual-dispatch row Icarus builds is *wrong* — through a base handle, through an argument, inside a fork, across a level that does not override, from a base method, with the override declared without the keyword, and a `clone` that returns the base type — which is what a tool that ignores `virtual` looks like measured; its own tracker records the mechanism and a comment that virtual methods would need changes in its runtime as well [@icarus-issue-421; @icarus-issue-292]. A class-handle `$cast` was proposed and closed without merging [@icarus-pr-1447]; the assignment of a derived handle to a base one is a still-open issue there, though the release this book runs elaborated it [@icarus-issue-422]. And Verilator, which runs every other row, has the one `new src` cell discussed above.

::: {.callout-tip title="In Practice"}
Composition is the row a reader will not think to look up. A method called through a handle-typed property — `env.drv.run()`, the ordinary shape of every environment ever written — does not compile on the event-driven tool. The worked example below cannot run there: it fails first on its interface port and clocking block, as @sec-ch05-tools's table predicts, and would fail on its composition next. The chapter says so rather than showing three silent passes. A parser that accepts the whole language elaborates every probe in this table without complaint, which is the lint pass @sec-ch05-tools recommended and the reason it is not a simulator.
:::

## Worked example: one environment, three tests {#sec-ch06-example}

::: {.callout-note title="Worked Example"}
An environment for the FIFO of @sec-ch01, written once: a transaction with a virtual contract, a factory, a callback hook, a driver whose `run` is a template method with a virtual step, and a scoreboard. Three tests each fill one hole — the factory substitutes a derived transaction with a stricter contract, an override changes one step, the callback attaches a count the driver knows nothing about — and the environment file is never edited.
:::

The environment. Each class has one hole, and the comment at the top names it:

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch06-oop-testbench-design/fifo-env/env.sv"}
```

The three tests, each a derived class that fills one hole. The even packet is a subtype in the sense this chapter uses: everything it produces is a legal packet, and its `legal` is stricter, not looser:

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch06-oop-testbench-design/fifo-env/tests.sv"}
```

The testbench builds the environment once and runs each test by choosing which maker, which driver and which callback to construct:

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch06-oop-testbench-design/fifo-env/tb_fifo_env.sv"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch06-oop-testbench-design/fifo-env/run.out"}
```

Three tests, three holes, zero edits to the environment, and the callback's count is evidence the third test collected from a driver it never subclassed. Read the override test's line once more: it rotated every packet's kind before sending, and the scoreboard still reports zero errors — because the scoreboard compares against what the driver *sent*, which the hook changed too. Whether that is what the test meant is a question about the test, and @sec-ch06-lsp is where the answer comes from.

::: {.callout-important title="Future Directions"}
The substitution property is the thing a program can check about generated test code. An agent that derives a transaction class can be asked, mechanically, whether the derived class still randomizes to a legal transaction and whether its overrides still call `super`; a parser that elaborates the whole language can answer the first for any constraint set and the second by reading the override. And the *wrong* cells in the table above are a specification: for a flow that runs on that tool, they are the constructs an agent must refuse to emit, because a testbench that uses them there will report success for tests it did not run. Both are checks a program can make before a person has to.
:::

## Summary

- A derived constructor reaches the base's first: `super.new` as the first statement, or an implicit no-argument call when it says nothing. The standard also lets the `extends` clause carry the arguments; the measured Verilator does not parse that form.
- Without `virtual` a redeclared method hides; with it, it overrides, and a call dispatches on the object rather than the handle. The template method — a base algorithm calling virtual steps — is what that rule is for.
- Do not call a virtual method from a constructor.
- Extend one base for shared state and code; implement any number of interface classes for a shared contract.
- `$cast` answers the down-cast question at run time and says no with a zero. `new src` copies the handle's declared type on this book's Verilator; a clone is a virtual method that constructs its own class.
- Every specialization of a parameterized class is a distinct type, with its own statics, its own factory registration and its own configuration pool.
- One idea under five patterns: a base class fixes an algorithm and leaves named holes — which class, what a step does, knob values, behavior in a component the test does not own, one of something.
- A subclass is a subtype when it can stand in for the base without the program telling; stricter constraints keep that, looser ones and forgotten `super` calls break it, and the factory cannot tell the difference.
- The event-driven simulator ignores `virtual` and refuses composition; this chapter's examples run on Verilator, and the table says which cells are silently wrong on each.

## Exercises

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise"}
1. Remove `virtual` from the template method's `step` and run the example on both simulators. Explain why the outputs now agree, and why that is worse.
2. Write a derived packet whose constructor forces the reserved kind that `packet::legal` rejects, and a maker that produces it. Show that the factory substitutes it without complaint, and read what the scoreboard says.
3. Replace `clone` in the cast-and-clone example with `new src` throughout and find the line of output that changes. Say which Verilator release would change it back.
4. Give `box #(T)` a static queue of every value ever boxed and show, with two specializations, that there are two queues.
5. Turn the override test into a strategy in the chapter's sense — a `send_policy` object with a virtual method that the test hands in — and say what the environment had to expose, and how that differs from the callback only in who calls it.
6. Add a row to the support table for a construct not in it — a virtual method with a default argument, say — with its probe, and classify it.
:::

## Further reading

Spear and Tumbush's chapter titled "Advanced OOP and Testbench Guidelines" is the standard text's treatment of inheritance in a testbench [@spear2012svfv]. Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides is where the pattern names come from, and the book to read for the idea under them [@gamma1994patterns]. Liskov's 1987 keynote is the source of the substitution property, in her words [@liskov1987hierarchy]. The UVM 1.2 user guide and class reference are where the factory, the policies and the phases are specified for the library Part III uses [@accellera2015uvmug; @accellera2015uvmref], and the lowRISC DV style guide is a production statement of how they are used [@lowrisc-dv-style]. For what the two open simulators do, the Icarus tracker records what the tool ignores [@icarus-issue-421] and Verilator's change log records what 5.046 fixed [@verilator-changes]; the table above is the measurement of both.
